tagline: Castles, spires, and a hundred bridges
overview:
Czechia, also called the Czech Republic, is a landlocked country in the center of Europe, about the size of South Carolina, ringed by Germany, Poland, Slovakia, and Austria. Its capital, Prague, is one of the most visited cities in the world, a fairy tale of spires, a medieval astronomical clock, and a stone bridge lined with statues arching over the Vltava River. Around 10.9 million people live in the country, which is made up of three historic lands: Bohemia in the west, Moravia in the east, and a slice of Silesia in the north.

Czech is the official language, and Slovak, spoken in the neighboring country that was once joined with it, is understood by nearly everyone. Czechia is a parliamentary republic with a president and a prime minister, a member of the European Union since 2004 and of NATO since 1999. It is a highly industrial country, making cars, machines, and glass, and it has a long tradition of beer brewing, puppet theater, and classical music from composers like Dvořák and Smetana.
landAndNature: Czechia sits in a bowl. Bohemia is ringed by low mountain ranges, including the Krkonoše, or Giant Mountains, where Sněžka reaches 1,603 meters, and the forested Šumava along the Bavarian border, one of the largest wild areas in Central Europe. Inside the ring lie rolling hills, farmland, fishponds dug in the Middle Ages, and rivers such as the Vltava and Elbe. Moravia is gentler, with vineyards in the south and the karst caves of the Moravian Karst, including the Macocha Abyss, a sinkhole 138 meters deep. The Bohemian Switzerland park has sandstone towers and the largest natural rock arch in Europe. Lynx have returned to the Šumava, and storks nest on village chimneys. Winters are cold and snowy, summers warm.
peopleAndCulture: Czechs are known for dry humor and for drinking more beer per person than any other nation; Pilsner-style lager was invented in the city of Plzeň in 1842. Favorite foods include roast pork with dumplings and sauerkraut, svíčková, beef in a creamy vegetable sauce, and sweet fruit dumplings. Puppet theater is a treasured art, and Czech cartoons such as the Little Mole are loved across Europe. Ice hockey rivals soccer as the national sport, and Czech players fill professional leagues worldwide. Writers Franz Kafka and Milan Kundera, composer Antonín Dvořák, and film director Miloš Forman all came from here. Easter brings decorated eggs, and Christmas Eve dinner is traditionally fried carp, sold live from tubs on the streets.
history: Slavic tribes settled Bohemia and Moravia by the 500s, and the Great Moravian Empire flourished in the 800s. The Kingdom of Bohemia became powerful in the Middle Ages, and under Emperor Charles IV in the 1300s Prague was the capital of the Holy Roman Empire and got Central Europe's first university. Religious reformer Jan Hus was burned at the stake in 1415, sparking wars. From 1526 the Habsburgs of Austria ruled for almost 400 years. Czechoslovakia was born in 1918 after World War I, but Nazi Germany dismantled it in 1938 and 1939. After the war a communist government took over; the Prague Spring reforms of 1968 were crushed by Soviet tanks. The peaceful Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communism, and in 1993 Czechia and Slovakia split into two friendly countries.
funFacts: Prague's astronomical clock has struck the hour with parading apostle figures since 1410, making it the oldest still working.
The word robot was invented by Czech writer Karel Čapek for a 1920 play about artificial workers.
Czechs drink more beer per person than any other country, roughly 130 liters a year on average.
Prague Castle is the largest ancient castle complex in the world, covering about 70,000 square meters.
Contact lenses as we know them were developed by Czech chemist Otto Wichterle, who built his first machine from a child's construction kit.
